title: Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan attends SSUHS Convocation in Guwahati
subtitle:
Vice President urges healthcare professionals to combine compassion with scientific excellence and dedicate themselves to service of humanity

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visionary leadership has transformed India’s healthcare landscape: Vice President

Assam’s medical colleges more than doubled from 7 in 2021 to 15; 9 more under construction: Vice President lauds CM Himanta Biswa Sarma

AIIMS Guwahati and three-tier cancer-care network strengthening Northeast’s healthcare ecosystem: Vice President

Vice President calls upon youth to stay away from substance abuse and contribute towards Nasha Mukt Bharat
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 6:05PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan today urged graduating healthcare professionals to uphold compassion, ethics and scientific excellence, and dedicate their knowledge and skills to the service of humanity, while addressing the convocation ceremony of Srimanta Sankaradeva University of Health Sciences (SSUHS), Guwahati. He also presented the Dr. John Berry White Award for the years 2023, 2024 and 2025.
Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan graced the convocation ceremony of Srimanta Sankaradeva University of Health Sciences (SSUHS), Guwahati today.
The Vice President said that the University, named after Mahapurusha Srimanta Sankaradeva, has emerged as an important…

Addressing the convocation, he said that the University, named after Mahapurusha Srimanta Sankaradeva, has emerged as an important institution for health sciences education, research and public health. He appreciated its efforts to promote medical knowledge in local languages, including the publication of an Anglo-Assamese Dictionary of Medical Science and medical textbooks in Assamese.
The Vice President highlighted the transformation of India’s healthcare sector under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, referring to initiatives such as Ayushman Bharat. He noted that more than 44 crore Ayushman cards have been issued and recalled that the scheme has helped poor and middle-class families save an estimated Rs. 2 lakh crore in medical expenses.
Highlighting Assam’s healthcare progress, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan said that the number of medical colleges in the State has more than doubled from seven in 2021 to 15, with another nine under construction. He also highlighted AIIMS Guwahati, the first AIIMS in the Northeast, and Assam’s three-tier cancer-care network, including the State’s first Proton Beam Therapy Centre.
The Vice President congratulated Chief Minister Dr. Himanta Biswa Sarma and the Government of Assam for strengthening healthcare infrastructure and said that the changing healthcare landscape is enabling patients from outside Assam to increasingly seek advanced treatment in Guwahati.
Calling upon youth to lead healthy and disciplined lives, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan urged them to stay away from substance abuse and contribute towards building a Nasha Mukt Bharat. He also advised students to use social media constructively and not allow it to consume excessive time.
The Vice President said that young healthcare professionals have a crucial role in advancing the vision of a Viksit and Swasth Bharat, and wished the graduating students success in their future endeavours.
The convocation was attended by Governor of Assam Shri Lakshman Prasad Acharya; Chief Minister Dr. Himanta Biswa Sarma; Minister of Medical Education & Research Shri Ashok Singhal; Education Minister Dr. Ranoj Pegu; Chief Secretary Dr. Ravi Kota; Vice-Chancellor of SSUHS Dr. Anup Kumar Barman, besides faculty members, researchers, students and parents.

title: Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi addresses  gathering at the inauguration of BAPS Swaminarayan Hindu Mandir in Paris
subtitle:
It is a matter of great joy that BAPS Swaminarayan Hindu Mandir is being inaugurated in Paris: PM

This temple will surely enrich the diversity of France and energize our cultural relations: PM

India-France Strategic Partnership is special as it rests on the strong foundation of old cultural and political bonds: PM
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 11:59PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi addressed a gathering through a video conference during the inauguration of BAPS Swaminarayan Hindu Mandir in Paris . Highlighting the monumental inauguration taking place in the French capital, the Prime Minister recognized the historic event as a foundational pillar for bilateral ties. “This grand Swaminarayan Temple is a new milestone in the cultural relations between India and France,” noted Shri Modi.
Invoking the blessings of revered saints and Sanatan tradition luminaries, the Prime Minister described the event's atmosphere as a true reflection of universal brotherhood. He emphasized that this gathering embodies ancient philosophies on a global stage. “Today, this stage has become an awakened platform for the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam,” observed Shri Modi.
Expressing deep gratitude for the divine grace and the affection of spiritual leaders, the Prime Minister reflected on his continued, fortunate association with such sacred milestones. “I continue to get the opportunity to associate with such pious occasions,” remarked Shri Modi.
Addressing the audience remotely, the Prime Minister conveyed his profound emotional connection to the ongoing festivities despite not being there in person. “In mind and spirit, I am experiencing myself right among you,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Paying respectful homage to Param Pujya Pramukh Swami Ji Maharaj, the Prime Minister recalled the visionary campaign launched to revive India's ancient cultural and spiritual glory. He noted how this global mission has gained immense momentum over the years. “Today, the light of that renaissance is spreading across the entire world, including Europe,” observed Shri Modi.
Tracing the journey from the grand Abu Dhabi temple inaugurated earlier in 2024 to the current marvel, the Prime Minister commended the relentless dedication and visionary efforts of the spiritual leaders. “This continuity of creation is a testament to the sheer resolve of the saints,” asserted Shri Modi.
Offering his deep reverence to Param Pujya Mahant Swami Maharaj, the Prime Minister extended heartfelt congratulations to the BAPS organization and its millions of followers. “I express my gratitude for this pious work,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Explaining how the global consecration of temples also exports India's ancient philosophy, the Prime Minister cited the guiding principle that calls for profound human unity. He emphasized that these core values naturally travel alongside the spiritual ceremonies. “India's thought advocates that our minds should be one and our hearts must connect,” noted Shri Modi.
Pointing out the broader societal impact, the Prime Minister emphasized that the magnificent structure would simultaneously enhance local cultural landscapes and supercharge bilateral ties. “This temple will surely enrich the diversity of France and energize our cultural relations,” asserted Shri Modi.
Reflecting on the soaring trajectory of diplomatic ties in recent years, the Prime Minister highlighted the collaborative, visionary efforts undertaken alongside President Emmanuel Macron. “Both countries are building a Special Global Strategic Partnership together,” noted Shri Modi.
Outlining the expansive scope of bilateral cooperation spanning AI, defense, space, and climate action, the Prime Minister pointed to the upcoming 2026 India-France Year of Innovation. He stated that these combined efforts are unlocking unprecedented technological advancements. “We are moving forward together with a new momentum and new energy,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Underscoring the uniqueness of this modern alliance, the Prime Minister attributed its contemporary strength to the enduring historical ties shared by both nations. “This Strategic Partnership is special because it rests on the strong foundation of our old cultural and political bonds,” observed Shri Modi.
Recalling the valor of Indian soldiers on French soil, the Prime Minister also praised the pivotal role played by French scholars in elevating a classical Indian language on the global stage. “They have played an incredibly important role in popularizing Sanskrit,” noted Shri Modi.
Delving into literary and spiritual exchanges, the Prime Minister cited Romain Rolland’s writings on Indian mystics and The Mother’s transformative journey to Puducherry as powerful catalysts for mutual inspiration. He acknowledged how these intellectual pursuits have deeply inspired seekers from both countries. “These spiritual connections have brought our societies much closer over the years,” remarked Shri Modi.
Looking back at the historical milestones of faith, the Prime Minister highlighted the arrival of a prominent spiritual leader in France decades ago. “Through ISKCON, Srila Prabhupada Swami started a new chapter of spiritual relations,” observed Shri Modi.
Drawing parallels between the widespread embrace of Yoga near the Eiffel Tower and the new temple, the Prime Minister identified these as powerful mediums for people-to-people connectivity. “A new chapter is being added to our cultural relations through this grand, divine temple,” asserted Shri Modi.
Weaving economic terminology into the spiritual narrative, the Prime Minister playfully compared the temple's creation to modern bilateral enterprise discussions. “The Swaminarayan Temple has added a completely new dimension to the possibilities of joint ventures,” remarked Shri Modi.
Detailing the architectural synthesis, the Prime Minister explained how ancient Indian carving talent seamlessly integrated with modern French engineering to shape the magnificent structure. He highlighted the careful craftsmanship applied to the stones sent from India. “This temple is truly 'Made in India' and 'Built in France',” noted Shri Modi.
Casting a visionary gaze toward the future, the Prime Minister expressed supreme confidence in the enduring legacy of this collaborative architectural marvel. “It will remain a symbol of cooperation and possibilities between India and France for centuries to come,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Reinforcing the dual mission of spiritual practice and social welfare inherent in these institutions, the Prime Minister expressed optimism about the site's upcoming humanitarian projects. “Swaminarayan temples have always been a medium of service along with devotion,” observed Shri Modi.
Projecting the regional impact of the center, the Prime Minister anticipated that the resonant values of Indian heritage would uplift the broader continent. He expressed certainty that these teachings would resonate far beyond Paris. “The voices of Indian culture emerging from here will benefit people across the whole of Europe,” asserted Shri Modi. “In the future, whenever I get the time, I will try to visit this temple for darshan,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Concluding his address with immense goodwill, the Prime Minister extended his best wishes toward the attendees, families, devotees, and the entire diaspora celebrating the inauguration.

content:
Respected Mahant Swami, honored representatives of the French government, distinguished guests, members of the Indian community, all Hari devotees connected from across the world, ladies and gentlemen - Jai Swaminarayan!
Today, in the capital of France, Paris, the grand Swaminarayan temple is being inaugurated. This inauguration is a new milestone in the cultural relations between India and France. With the blessings of revered saints and the noble custodians of the Sanatan tradition, today this inauguration platform has become a stage of the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam - “the world is one family.” By the grace of Lord Swaminarayan and the affection and blessings of our saints, it is my fortune that I always get the opportunity to be connected with such sacred occasions. Even today, though I am not physically present among you in Paris, in mind and heart I feel myself to be right there with you.
Friends,
On this occasion, I also respectfully remember Param Pujya Pramukh Swami Maharaj. In ancient times, India’s cultural and spiritual glory was immense, and he began a campaign for its renaissance. Today its light is spreading across Europe and the entire world. In 2024, the grand temple in Abu Dhabi was inaugurated. Today thousands of people go there for darshan. And now here in Paris, the construction of the Swaminarayan temple - this continuity of creation - is proof of the resolve and strength of our saints. I express gratitude to Pujya Mahant Swami for this sacred work, I bow at his feet. I extend heartfelt congratulations to the BAPS Swaminarayan organization and to millions of Hari devotees on this occasion.
Friends,
Through BAPS, when temples are consecrated in different countries, India’s ancient ideas and human values also travel with them. And India’s thought says: “Samanam manah saha chittamesham” - may our minds be united, may our hearts be connected. Therefore, today when such a grand temple has been built in France, it will enrich France’s diversity, and it will also energize the cultural relations between India and France.
Friends,
In recent years, India and France’s relations have reached new heights. Together with my friend President Macron, both countries are building a Special Global Strategic Partnership. From technology, AI, and defense to space and climate action, we are moving forward with new speed and new energy. We are also celebrating 2026 as the India–France Year of Innovation. This strategic partnership is special because it rests on the strong foundation of our old cultural and political ties. History is witness - the sacrifices of Indian soldiers in France are still alive in the temple of memory. Those interested in languages also know how French scholars played a crucial role in popularizing Sanskrit. The writings of Romain Rolland on Ramakrishna Paramhansa and Swami Vivekananda brought our societies closer. From Paris to the Puducherry Aurobindo Ashram, “The Mother’s” spiritual journey inspired countless Indian and French seekers.
Friends,
Decades ago, Srila Prabhupada Swami also came to France. Through ISKCON he began a new chapter of spiritual relations between India and France. Today yoga too has become a medium of people‑to‑people connection between India and France. The pictures from in front of the Eiffel Tower on International Yoga Day are examples of yoga’s popularity in France. And now, through this grand BAPS temple, a new chapter is being added to our cultural relations.
Friends,
These days, there are discussions about India–France joint ventures. The Swaminarayan temple has added a new dimension to this possibility. This temple is “Made in India” and “Built in France.” Many of its stones were carved in India. India’s ancient craftsmanship has joined here with modern engineering in France. In Paris, this grand temple has taken shape. Therefore, I hope this temple will stand for centuries as a symbol of cooperation and possibilities between India and France.
Friends,
Swaminarayan temples have always been not only centers of devotion but also of service. I have been told that this temple too will become such a center of service projects. I am confident that the voices of Indian culture that will arise from here will benefit people across Europe. In the future, whenever I get the time, I will surely make the effort to come and have darshan in this temple. With these words, once again I extend many congratulations on this auspicious occasion to all the guests present, all families, all Hari devotees, and the entire Indian diaspora.
Thank you very much!
Merci beaucoup!
Jai Swaminarayan!

title: Adequate Coal for Punjab's Power Plants: Centre enabled Supply from PSPCL's Captive Mines Since Commencement of its captive Mine Production
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 2:37PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Media reports attributing reduced power generation at Punjab's thermal plants to inadequate coal supply from the Centre do not present the complete picture. The Ministry of Coal clarifies that adequate coal has been made available to Punjab's power plants, and Coal India Limited (CIL) remains fully committed to ensuring uninterrupted coal supply for power generation across the country, including in the State of Punjab.
Central Government’s support to Punjab's coal supply chain
The Central Government proactively facilitated coal movement to Independent Power Plants (IPPs) in Punjab, since commencement of its captive mine production.
Supply of coal from PSPCL's captive Pachhwara Central Coal Mine to IPPs enabled, subject to fulfilment of the statutory payment obligation to the State of Jharkhand.
Utilisation of coal from the Pachhwara Central Coal Mine by IPPs not owned by PSPCL, including Nabha Power Limited (Rajpura) and Talwandi Sabo Power Limited (Mansa), is already allowed upto 50% of annual production after meeting the requirements of Specified End Use Plants.
Coal India Limited (CIL) support to Punjab and lower PLF (42%) of PSPCL’s plants
PSPCL operates three thermal power plants — Guru Hargobind TPS (Lehra Mohabbat), Goindwal Sahib TPP, and Ropar TPS — with a combined capacity of 2,300 MW. As on 04.09.2026, coal stock at PSPCL's plants stood at around 117% of the normative requirement, reflecting more than adequate coal availability. Despite this comfortable stock position, the average Plant Load Factor (PLF) of PSPCL's plants during August 2026 was only around 42%. The low generation during the month therefore cannot be attributed to inadequate coal availability at the plant end.
In contrast, Nabha Power Limited, a Punjab-based IPP, achieved a PLF of around 93% during the same period, backed by adequate coal supplies from CIL sources, demonstrating that coal availability has not been a constraint for power generation in the State.
IPPs Need to Improve Lifting of Coal Already Offered by CIL
Coal India subsidiaries have proactively offered coal to Punjab-based IPPs, though booking and lifting have lagged:
CCL offered 5 lakh tonnes (LT) of coal to NPL and TSPL on 30.03.2026 under RCR mode. Of this, only about 4.1 LT has been booked and around 3.1 LT lifted so far.
BCCL offered 3.5 LT of coal to NPL, against which only around 1.3 LT has been booked and 0.98 LT lifted so far.
The timely lifting of coal by the IPPs, together with improved generation performance at PSPCL's own plants, are equally critical to optimising power generation in Punjab.
The Ministry of Coal reiterates that the Central Government has already taken concrete steps to enable coal movement to Punjab's IPPs from PSPCL's captive mines. Coal India Limited remains committed to maintaining uninterrupted coal supply for power generation nationwide, including in Punjab. Higher utilisation of PSPCL's own plants, coupled with timely lifting of the coal already offered by CIL subsidiaries, would help optimise power generation and address the State's power requirements.

title: India Must Build Resilient, Globally Integrated Healthcare Supply Chains: Commerce and Industry Minister Shri Piyush Goyal at Bharat Health Global Expo 2026
subtitle:
Pharma sector must lead in R&D, new molecules, biosimilars and biotech: Shri Goyal

India must adopt an outward-looking approach to supply-chain resilience, including investments in overseas markets for local value addition and last-mile delivery: Shri Goyal

Government ready to support medical value travel, pharma and healthcare infrastructure and sector-specific plug-and-play industrial facilities
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 9:28PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India must build resilient, globally integrated healthcare supply chains, strengthen its position as a trusted healthcare partner of the world and move beyond its success in generics towards greater research, development and innovation, said Union Minister of Commerce & Industry Shri Piyush Goyal at the Bharat Health Global Expo 2026 in New Delhi today.
The Minister attended the Expo along with Minister of State for Commerce and Industry and Electronics and Information Technology Shri Jitin Prasada and Commerce Secretary Shri Rajesh Agarwal
Shri Goyal said that India’s pharmaceutical sector has a significant opportunity to showcase its capabilities to the world and that the country, known as the “pharmacy of the world”, must aim for a much bigger and better future. He said that the coming together of the healthcare community through Bharat Health Global Expo marks only the beginning and has significant potential, with the entire value chain being brought together on a single platform to encourage greater international participation.
The Minister said that at a later stage, the platform could also be opened for country pavilions and partner countries, allowing foreign companies to showcase their products alongside Indian companies. He said this would enable India to demonstrate its capabilities with confidence and compete with the best globally.
Highlighting the importance of resilience in supply chains, Shri Goyal said that the world is increasingly looking for resilient supply chains and is not comfortable with excessive geographical dependence on one or two locations or with supply chains that could potentially be weaponised. He noted that India had earlier lost ground in Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) and Key Starting Materials (KSMs) for a variety of reasons and said that it was now time to restore resilience in the pharmaceutical supply chain.
He clarified that resilience should not mean an inward-looking approach. He said that India does not need to indigenise everything and that imports would continue to be necessary where required. However, products should be available from multiple geographies and companies so that no one or two countries or companies can hold businesses to ransom and threaten the continuity of the industry.
Shri Goyal said that pooling India’s demand would identify several products currently imported where there is potential for indigenous production. He added that countries across the world are now competing to attract investment and build resilience in their supply chains.
He noted that the competition for investment is no longer limited to developing countries, with the United States, Canada, Mexico, Japan, Korea, Singapore, Europe and other developed economies also seeking to attract investments to their geographies. He said that India is therefore competing not only in goods and services but also with developed countries in attracting investment, making the task of strengthening India’s investment proposition even more important.
At the same time, Shri Goyal said that India must recognise that other countries are also seeking resilience and therefore the pharmaceutical sector would need to adopt a global and outward-looking approach. He said there may be countries where Indian pharmaceutical companies need to invest for last-mile delivery, local value addition and job creation, including in African countries. He emphasised that the sector would need to adopt a global outlook in the years ahead.
On research and development and innovation, Shri Goyal said that India’s success in generics has been built through the active and sustained efforts of the pharmaceutical industry. However, he said India cannot rest its case with generics if it aims to become a developed country by 2047.
Shri Goyal said India must promote greater R&D, develop and patent its own products, and make use of programmes launched to support R&D and innovation. He added that the pharmaceutical sector should be at the forefront of R&D and leverage initiatives such as the Research and Development Innovation Fund (RDIF). He called for Indian companies, engineers and talent to focus on new molecules, biosimilars and biotechnology, which he said should become the next frontier for the sector.
Shri Goyal said India would also have to offer the world a regulatory mechanism that makes R&D and innovation attractive in the country. He called for an open and inviting approach towards investment in clinical trials, patenting products, conducting R&D and introducing new products in India.
He said that Indian regulators should examine regulations in more developed countries and take cues from global developments to move towards greater regulatory convergence with the developed world. He stressed that unless India’s mindset and approach align with the developed world, the country cannot aim to become a developed country by 2047. He said that India must listen to investors willing to come to the country and to the demands of governments globally, and together craft a new pathway for the success of the industry.
On medical value travel, Shri Goyal said that almost USD 8 billion is spent in this area and highlighted that Indian hospitals have become modern and world-class, with the best of equipment, while Indian doctors, technicians and nurses are among the best. He called for medical value travel to be taken up on a mission mode.
He said that SEPC has already undertaken initiatives with CII, FICCI and others in this area and called for efforts to capture a greater share of the market and promote the Indian healthcare story globally. He said that through the EPM and India Brand Equity Fund, the Government would be happy to support initiatives to promote medical care in India for the rest of the world and urged the industry to come forward with proposals quickly.
The Minister said that India’s role as a trusted partner of the world, particularly in healthcare, has been demonstrated repeatedly through the COVID pandemic, the provision of generics across the world and the emergence of new innovations and patented products from India. He said that these developments, collectively, would help take the industry to the next level both domestically and globally.
Shri Goyal said that the last 40 years have been a defining period for the pharmaceutical industry but the sector should not be content with where it stands today. He called upon the industry to “aim for the skies” and work towards a much bigger and better future.
On infrastructure, Shri Goyal said that the Government has been working to develop bulk drug parks, with projects coming up in Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat and Himachal Pradesh, including both old and new parks. He said that 100 new industrial parks are coming up where dedicated areas can be provided for the pharma and healthcare sector, if required.
He similarly invited the industry in sectors such as engineering, aerospace and defence to be more demanding about locations where they wish to establish their industries. He said the Government would be happy to create plug-and-play infrastructure suited to the requirements of different sectors.
On medical devices, Shri Goyal said that while there have been efforts in the sector, India still has a long way to go. He called for a shift from assemblies towards domestic and indigenous production of components and the entire medical devices ecosystem, noting that there remains significant scope for growth in medical devices.
He said that doctors, nurses, technicians and hospitals would have to become more conscious about the availability of better and superior products in India. Greater domestic market share would also support exports, as the large Indian market can provide economies of scale. He said MSMEs can support the indigenisation of components and equipment, while larger companies can create scale.
Shri Goyal said that collectively these efforts can create millions of jobs, promote investments worth billions of dollars and make India more resilient against future crises.
On Ayush, Shri Goyal said that it represents India’s traditional medicine and traditional wisdom, but India is still exporting raw herbs. He called for greater scientific validation of Ayush products so that they can gain wider acceptance globally, noting that the Government has already been working in this direction.
Highlighting the importance of collaboration, Shri Goyal said that India has planned several similar initiatives in areas of its strength, with the pharmaceutical sector being one of the country’s biggest strengths. He said it was important to bring the sector together on a single platform rather than having separate conferences for different segments. He noted that a unified platform could attract participation from 50 countries and around 1,000 people from across the world, while enabling stakeholders to get a comprehensive view of developments across the sector and compare and identify the best.
The Minister said India too must have the courage of conviction that it can compete with the best. He said competition would ultimately be determined by quality, timely delivery and good customer service. He said India has the opportunity and the capability, particularly in the health sector, to showcase the best to the world.
On international market access, Shri Goyal said FTAs were opening up global markets for Indian industry and that almost two-thirds of the global market is already open for preferential market access for India. He said India is negotiating another 8 to 10 multilateral or bilateral FTAs or PTAs, which would provide access to almost 75 per cent of global trade.
He said that, until 2014, India’s FTAs collectively provided access to markets with a combined GDP of USD 10 trillion. In contrast, the nine FTAs referred to by Shri Jitin Prasada and covered in the accompanying book cover 38 developed countries and open access to a combined GDP of USD 60 trillion, six times more than what was open until 2014. He noted that many of these FTAs had remained stuck for 25 years.
Shri Goyal said Indian industry is competitive and best in class, with strong talent, and that what is needed now is greater ambition, higher goals and the ability to connect the dots. He said an organisation such as Bharat Health is attempting to do precisely this by bringing different organisations together, getting everyone on the same page and encouraging collaboration and cooperation.
He said healthy competition is necessary and good, but the sector must also collaborate. He called upon the industry to aim big, adopt a modern outlook, go global, make quality its top priority, build resilience and scale, invest in R&D and innovation, leverage Indian capabilities and talent, and make full use of the opportunities being opened through India’s trade partnerships.
Shri Goyal called upon the industry to earn greater trust, goodwill and market share across the world and work towards making India the “health stack for the globe”. He said no human being, economy or country can be successful or happy without high-quality healthcare.
The Minister said that Viksit Bharat 2047 rests on the shoulders of the healthcare sector, which has the responsibility of providing a healthy India, ensuring good health facilities and quality medicines, and delivering both preventive wellness and curative healthcare to 1.4 billion people. He said this would be the mainstay of Viksit Bharat 2047.

title: National Zoological Park Organises Sunday Bird, Butterfly and Dragonfly Walks to Promote Science and Biodiversity Conservation among Citizens
ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 7:16PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Zoological Park (NZP), New Delhi, organised the third ‘Butterfly and Dragonfly Walk @ NZP’ and the 13th ‘Sunday Bird Walk @ NZP’, as part of its ongoing efforts to promote public participation in biodiversity monitoring, documentation of birds, butterflies and dragonflies, and awareness of wildlife conservation. The walks were conducted from 6:45 AM to 10:30 AM today under the expert guidance of Sh. Sanjay Tiwari and Sh. C.B. Maurya, butterfly and dragonfly expert, along with dedicated volunteers.
The programme received an enthusiastic response from bird and butterfly enthusiasts, nature lovers, students, wildlife photographers and citizens interested in biodiversity conservation. A total of 16 participants took part in the walks. The event was attended by the Director, National Zoological Park, zoo officials and resource experts, who guided and interacted with participants throughout the activity. During the walks, participants documented 44 bird species, with observations of more than 700 individual birds, along with 4 butterfly species, one dragonfly and one damselfly species each in the walk area. The relatively lower number of butterflies and dragonflies recorded was attributed to intermittent rainfall.
A notable highlight of the Bird Walk was the presence of more than 300 Painted Storks, which arrived at the National Zoological Park during the second week of August and have begun nesting on trees in and around the pond. Their arrival and nesting are encouraging indicators of the ecological value of the Zoo’s wetland and tree habitats. The nesting activity and breeding behaviour also provide an important opportunity for visitors, interns, volunteers and citizen scientists to observe and better understand natural bird behaviour and breeding ecology.
Sh. C.B. Maurya shared valuable insights into the ecology, behaviour and conservation of birds, butterflies and dragonflies, highlighting their vital ecological roles as pollinators, natural pest controllers and indicators of ecosystem health. The programme provided participants with an opportunity to connect with nature, enhance their species-identification skills and develop a deeper appreciation of biodiversity and its conservation.
Addressing the participants, Dr. Sanjeet Kumar, Director, National Zoological Park, highlighted that such nature walks provide valuable opportunities to strengthen field-identification skills, improve understanding of food webs, contribute to biodiversity documentation and foster a deeper appreciation of wildlife and biodiversity conservation. The programme concluded with an interactive discussion, a participant feedback session and a group photograph with the experts and zoo officials.
Participation in each Sunday Nature Walk is limited to 20–25 participants to ensure a meaningful and high-quality learning experience. Prior registration is mandatory and is accepted on a first-come, first-served basis. Interested participants may register through the designated Google Form, which remains open from Monday to Friday each week. The registration link is available on the official website of the National Zoological Park, New Delhi, and through the “NZP Sathi” mobile application.
The next nature walks—the 3rd ‘Sunday Insect and Spider Walk’ and the 14th ‘Sunday Bird Walk’—are scheduled to be held on Sunday, 20 September 2026.

Dynamic Local Level Planning imperative for documenting Local Biodiversity and Traditional Knowledge that contribute to Sustainable Development: Shri Bhupender Yadav

content:
Chandigarh/New Delhi, 6th September, 2026
The 16th National Meet of the State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) and Union Territory Biodiversity Councils (UTBCs) was inaugurated today at Chandigarh. Organised by the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), the two-day National Meet, being held from 6–7 September 2026, brings together Chairpersons and Member Secretaries of SBBs and UTBCs from across the country, along with senior officials, experts and scientists.
The inaugural session was presided over by Governor of Punjab and Administrator, UT Chandigarh, Shri Gulab Chand Kataria; Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav; and Minister for Environment, Forest and Wildlife, Government of Haryana, Shri Rao Narbir Singh. Other dignitaries present in the occasion included Secretary, MoEFCC, Shri Tanmay Kumar; Director General of Forests and Special Secretary, MoEFCC, Shri Sushil Kumar Awasthi; Additional Secretary (MoEFCC), Shri Ashutosh Agnihotri; Chairperson, National Biodiversity Airport (NBA), Shri Virendra Tiwari; and other senior officials of the Union Ministry, besides those from SBBs and UTBCs.
Addressing the gathering, Shri Gulab Chand Kataria highlighted India’s rich biological heritage and traditional environmental ethos. He emphasised that ecological security is closely linked with food and water security, livelihoods and sustainable development, and underlined the importance of combining traditional knowledge and community participation with contemporary approaches. The Governor drew attention to the ecological significance of its wetlands, riverine ecosystems and agricultural biodiversity. He stressed the importance of strengthening Biodiversity Management Committees and People’s Biodiversity Registers and called for stronger coordination among biodiversity institutions and local communities.
In his address on the occasion, Shri Bhupender Yadav highlighted India’s long-standing environmental ethos and referred to initiatives under the vision of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi like Mission LiFE, Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam, Amrit Sarovar and the Green Credit Programme. India takes along its scientific prowess as well as traditional community wisdom together in this conservation journey, he stated. Referring to the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, the Minister noted that the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 and the Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 have further strengthened and streamlined the biodiversity governance framework. He urged States and Union Territories to align their rules, institutional mechanisms and implementation processes with the amended framework.
The Minister appreciated India’s progress in fulfilling its international biodiversity commitments, including the submission of the 7th National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity and the 1st National Report on the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing. Emphasising implementation at the grassroots level, Shri Yadav called for making the more than 2.76 lakh Biodiversity Management Committees functional and effective. He also called for People’s Biodiversity Registers to evolve into dynamic planning instruments for local bodies, enabling information on local biodiversity and associated traditional knowledge to contribute to local planning and sustainable development.
On Access and Benefit Sharing, the Minister noted that the National Biodiversity Authority has shared over ₹200 crore of ABS funds with farmers, local communities, Biodiversity Management Committees, State Biodiversity Boards, Union Territory Biodiversity Councils and research institutions. He emphasised that ABS should deliver tangible benefits to communities while contributing to conservation and sustainable livelihoods. The event saw the release of knowledge products, including the document on last one year achievements of the NBA, giving an overview of the ABS scheme and efficient distribution of these funds among the stakeholders.
Highlighting the linkages between biodiversity and climate action, Shri Bhupender Yadav referred to how over the years India has regularly taken decisive steps aligned with International protocols in the field of biodiversity conservation, while following a ‘Whole of Government’and ‘Whole of Society’ approaches. He talked about India's Updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) 2024–2030, which is aligned with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). He called for measurable outcomes in ecosystem restoration, species and habitat conservation, agro-biodiversity and climate-resilient landscapes. He also encouraged States and UTs to become partners in contributing to the global 30-by-30 conservation target.
Speaking on the occasion, Shri Rao Narbir Singh, highlighted Haryana’s efforts towards conservation and restoration and emphasised the importance of strengthening biodiversity governance at the State and local levels. He highlighted the role of Biodiversity Management Committees in Haryana in conserving local biodiversity and called for enhanced training and capacity building of BMCs and local communities.
The two-day National Meet would provide a platform for States and Union Territories to share experiences, innovations and implementation challenges and to deliberate on practical measures for strengthening biodiversity governance. The deliberations are expected to contribute to stronger institutional mechanisms, improved functioning of Biodiversity Management Committees, better quality and utilisation of People’s Biodiversity Registers, enhanced capacity building and more effective implementation of the biodiversity governance framework at the State and local levels.

title: Union Environment Minister leads International Vulture Awareness Day 2026 celebrations and inaugurates National Workshop themed ‘From Crisis to Recovery – Conserving India’s Vultures’, at Panchkula
subtitle: Shri Bhupender Yadav calls for continued creation of Vulture Safe Zones and development of Technical Capacity to aid Species Recovery in the Wild
ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 10:49AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The International Vulture Awareness Day 2026 was celebrated today at Panchkula, Haryana. Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav inaugurated a national-level workshop on the theme ‘From Crisis to Recovery – Conserving India’s Vultures’ on the occasion. The event was also graced by the august presence of Haryana State Minister for Environment, Forest and Wildlife, Shri Rao Narbir Singh, besides senior dignitaries from the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), and Haryana State Government.
The programme was organised in collaboration with the MoEFCC, Central Zoo Authority (CZA), Haryana Forest & Wildlife Department, Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) and the Jatayu Conservation Breeding Centre (JCBC), Pinjore. It brought together senior forest officials, scientists, veterinarians, zoo professionals, conservation practitioners and other stakeholders to strengthen collaborative efforts for vulture conservation in India.
Addressing the gathering, Shri Yadav highlighted that the government's environment conservation approach, under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi,  is based on a holistic ecosystem-oriented conservation model and not limited to a particular species. The Minister stated the approach is evident in various species conservation initiatives whether it is Big Cats, Sloth Bear, Great Indian Bustard, Dolphins, Gharial, Wild water buffalo or Vultures. Talking about vultures, he informed how India, which is home to a diverse community resident and migratory vultures - White-rumped, Long-billed, Slender-billed, Red-headed, Egyptian, Himalayan Griffon, Eurasian Griffon, Cinereous and Bearded Vultures - is making efforts towards their successful conservation.
Shri Yadav highlighted the vital ecological role of vultures as highly efficient scavengers and described them as nature’s own cleaning system. By rapidly consuming animal carcasses, vultures facilitate nutrient recycling and help maintain ecological balance. He stated that world is facing challenges like Climate Change, Human-animal conflict and a sharp decline was observed in Indian Vulture population since 1990s mainly due to disruption in their food chain and use of pain killers for animals that were consumed by the vultures.
The Minister emphasised on coordinated efforts as a 'Whole of Government' and 'Whole of Society' approach in policy making for Vulture conservation. He called for continued efforts to create Vulture Safe Zones through vulture-safe veterinary practices, ensuring safe food availability and technical capacity building to aid species recovery in the wild. The Minister also appealed to veterinary professionals, livestock owners, local administrations and communities to actively contribute to vulture conservation and promote safe carcass-management practices.
Earlier, the Union Minister started the day with a visit to the JCBC Pinjore, where he visited the facility, reviewed a presentation on the Centre and interacted with officials involved in vulture conservation. The Centre, a collaborative initiative of the Haryana Forest Department and BNHS, has emerged as an important centre for conservation breeding of the White-rumped, Long-billed and Slender-billed Vultures.
It was informed that the Centre undertakes scientific husbandry, artificial incubation, veterinary care, breeding and genetic management. During 2025–26, JCBC housed 356 vultures and successfully bred 35 chicks. It also released or contributed 87 vultures for reintroduction, transferred 90 birds to other conservation-breeding institutions, and trained 1,222 participants from 22 institutions, thereby strengthening technical capacity for vulture conservation.
Addressing the gathering on the occasion, Shri Rao Narbir Singh talked about the important contribution and successful vulture conservation programme being carried out at the Jatayu Conservation Breeding Centre (JCBC), Pinjore. He emphasised that the success of conservation breeding should not be measured merely by the number of animals born, but by the establishment of healthy and genetically managed populations, generation of scientific knowledge, development of technical capacity and contribution towards species recovery in the wild.
During the inaugural session, a Coffee table book - 'Story of Jatayu: Saving India's Vulture' - was released on the occasion. It chronicles India's remarkable vulture conservation story from a declining Vulture population to the successful breeding conservation programme through the establishment of JCBC Pinjore. Further, a prize distribution ceremony was held for the online drawing competition and digital photography competition held on Vulture Conservation.
The International Vulture Awareness Day 2026 National Workshop was organized with a renewed commitment to ensuring that vultures continue to thrive in India’s landscapes and perform their vital ecological role. The journey ‘From Crisis to Recovery’ reflects India’s collective commitment to vulture conservation through science, policy, conservation breeding, safe landscapes and community participation.

date:

                06 SEP 2026 6:38PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah today addressed a press conference on narcotics control in Panaji, the capital of Goa. On this occasion, Goa Chief Minister Shri Pramod Sawant was also present.
Addressing the press conference, Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah said that since Shri Narendra Modi became the Prime Minister, the Government of India has taken numerous steps to strengthen the country’s internal security. He said that when Modi Ji became the Prime Minister, the country was facing three formidable problems, which included rising terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir, Naxalism, and the unrest created by several armed organisations in the Northeast. In addition, on the internal security front, the country was also greatly troubled by several bomb blasts. There were large-scale movements regarding the safety of women. It was precisely during that period that Modi Ji assumed the office of the Prime Minister of the country. Looking back from 2019 to now under his leadership, the situation has changed significantly. After the abrogation of Article 370 in Jammu and Kashmir, the feeling of separatism has reduced considerably. The figures of terrorism are gradually shrinking and moving towards zero, and Jammu and Kashmir has progressed on the path of development. Successful efforts have also been made to bridge the mental distance that existed between Jammu and Kashmir and the rest of the country. The five-decade-old problem of Naxalism has today almost become a thing of the past. Most of the people who imagined the Red Corridor have today surrendered by laying down arms and are joining the mainstream. Similarly, in the Northeast as well, around 11,000 youth have laid down arms. The Government of India has signed more than 14 agreements with them, and today the Northeast is also progressing on the path of development. After 2019, a campaign has also been launched against fugitives who fled after committing crimes. From 2019 to July 2026, 274 fugitives have been extradited from 36 countries. These include people involved in serious crimes such as economic offences, terrorism, narcotics, and gang wars. All of them have been brought before the courts of India. In the last three years, 401 Red Corner Notices have been issued. In 2026 alone, up to July, the entire process of issuing 182 Red Corner Notices has been successfully completed. For this, a new system has been created in the form of ‘BHARATPOL’. More than 14 central agencies and the police of all states are connected to ‘BHARATPOL’. A well-organised mechanism has been prepared through ‘BHARATPOL’ for the extradition of fugitives from every state. From 2019 to 2026, properties worth approximately ₹17,874 crore belonging to fugitives have been sealed or confiscated. The new criminal laws and justice codes have also made the path of legal action against fugitives easier.
Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah said that a systematic mechanism has also been prepared for cyber crimes, which is being monitored by Prime Minister Modi Ji himself. Today, the 1930 helpline has become an effective medium for protection against cyber crimes. Success has been achieved in implementing the three new criminal laws up to the police station level through the Ministry of Home Affairs with the cooperation of the states. He said that he thanks the Chief Minister of Goa and the Goa Police for implementing the new Nayaya Sanhita and the three criminal laws in such a short time and raising the conviction rate in the state to 53.2 per cent. This means that there has been an increase of approximately 30 per cent in the rate of securing convictions in registered FIRs.
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that narcotics is a crime that can destroy our future generations. He said that the earnings from narcotics are also used for terrorism. The narco-terror module is active in many countries of the world, and the entire world is today grappling with this problem. He said that since 2019, we have put in place a robust system to curb it. For this, we have changed the systems, caught the networks, broken the financial chain, and also provided handholding to those addicted so as to free them from drugs. Shri Shah said that before 2014, this battle was fought in a piecemeal manner, and satisfaction was derived from making small seizures and catching small accused persons. But since 2019, the Modi government has made this subject a priority of national security. He said that the fight against drugs has moved beyond files and the actions of separate agencies and has now become a coordinated and continuous campaign at the national level.
Union Home Minister said that in 2019, a four-tier NCORD mechanism was created. A model for the formation of dedicated Anti-Narcotics Task Forces was sent to all states and Union Territories, and a Joint Coordination Committee was constituted. With the coordination of central agencies, state governments and their departments, a scientific method was adopted to address large networks, inter-state and international links, and operational gaps. The ‘1933’ Manas helpline was started for the rehabilitation of drug-addicted youth. The cadre of the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) was restructured. A national database of narcotics offenders was created through the NIDAAN portal. Using CCTNS data and integrated data fusion, a data-based map of hotspots, modus operandi and seizures across the country was prepared. A new concept of investigation was adopted with both Bottom-to-Top and Top-to-Bottom approaches. He said that now even if a small packet of drugs is seized, it is examined where it originated from in the country. Similarly, if a large consignment is seized at the border, it is traced how it was going to reach the youth in the form of small packets. In this way, reverse investigation of the entire network has been started.
Shri Amit Shah said that special emphasis was given to financial investigation and PIT-NDPS, and a high-level dedicated task force was constituted. Technology-based investigation was started against the dark net, encrypted communication, crypto transactions and dead drop delivery. Work began on creating a dedicated Dark Net-Crypto Cell in the ANTF. An inter-ministerial mechanism was also created for precursors and synthetic drugs. He said that these efforts have yielded good results. Shri Shah said that from 2004 to 2014, under the rule of the opposition party, 26 lakh kilograms of drugs were seized, valued at approximately ₹40,000 crore. On the other hand, from 2014 to 2026 under the leadership of Modi Ji, this seizure has increased to more than 1 crore 19 lakh kilograms, valued at approximately ₹1 lakh 89 thousand crore. He said that from 2004 to 2014, 3 lakh 36 thousand kilograms of drugs were destroyed, whereas in 2014-26, 48 lakh 68 thousand kilograms of drugs have been destroyed.
Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah said that 10 apex meetings, 7 executive meetings, 277 state-level meetings and 16,798 district-level meetings of NCORD have been held. Agreements have been signed with 46 countries for international cooperation. Under the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyan, 25 crore citizens have been contacted and administered the oath. Under treatment and rehabilitation, 5 lakh 70 thousand citizens have been made drug-free. In Goa also, action has increased approximately three times during the same period.
Shri Amit Shah said that a three-year roadmap from July 2026 to July 2029 has been prepared. A decision has been taken to achieve all targets in a time-bound manner. He said that we are advancing the fight against drugs as one of the biggest national battles of the country. He said that the goal of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi is that by 2047, a drug-free youth power should form the foundation of a developed India. To make this mission successful, the Ministry of Home Affairs and all state governments are working together. He said that the period from 2026 to 2029 has been declared as mission mode. Timelines have been fixed, different ministries have been made accountable, measurable outcomes have been decided, and quarterly reviews along with outcome-based accountability will be ensured. He said that this roadmap is based on four pillars. First—intelligence and operation-based enforcement; second—precursor and synthetic drugs control; third—demand and harm reduction; and fourth—capacity building and coordination. He said that all these pillars together will prepare dossiers of drug kingpins, coordinate on backward-forward linkages, and tighten the noose through financial investigation of every case involving commercial quantities. He said that the BSF, CISF, Indian Coast Guard, Customs and DRI will carry out risk-based profiling and install scanners at land borders, ports, airports and cargo for sharper surveillance. The Home Minister said that the CBI, Ministry of External Affairs and Interpol will bring back the fugitives. The Enforcement Directorate, Financial Intelligence Unit and the banking system will catch the money trail.
Shri Amit Shah said that through the NCC, NSS and My Bharat, lakhs of ‘Nashamukti Mitra’ will be prepared. He said that the Ministry of Education, Youth Affairs and Sports, along with educational institutions, are taking a resolve to make educational institutions drug-free. The Social Justice, Health Department and Jail Administration together are going to increase the number of de-addiction centres threefold to 1,751. Approximately 10,000 volunteers will serve in this campaign. For capacity building, 7 per cent central assistance will be provided to create fully equipped Anti-Narcotics Task Forces in every state by March 2027. The Ministry of Home Affairs will make arrangements for forensic reports to be received within 30 days. In these four pillars, 25 components and more than 200 action points have been fixed in a time-bound manner.

title: “Bring Industry Partners on Board from Day One”: Dr Jitendra Singh Calls for New Industry–R&D Partnership Model
subtitle:
Minister says early industry participation can make technologies market-ready and accelerate commercialisation

The Minister calls for industry-led common R&D platforms and continued government-industry engagement
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 5:30PM by PIB Delhi
content:
“The commercial arm should be in association with the lab right from day one.” With this message, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences and MoS PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances, Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, called for a fundamental shift in the way industry and research institutions work together, during an interaction with CEOs, CSOs and COOs of industries at the 6th RISE Conclave at CSIR-IICB, Kolkata. He said that potential commercial partners should be identified and associated at the project-planning stage itself so that market requirements and practical considerations can shape the technology while it is still under development.
Responding to an industry suggestion that commercial partners should be brought in at the laboratory stage, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that early participation would allow industry to provide inputs on market dynamics, design, environmental sustainability, supply-chain requirements and commercial viability. He said, stressing that a technology should not reach the market only to discover that it needs modification to meet actual user requirements.
The interaction thereafter became a direct platform for industry to place specific technology and challenges before the Minister.
Critical minerals and indigenous technology also emerged as major areas of industry interest, with participants discussing rare-earth extraction, permanent magnets, recycling, lithium beneficiation and the recovery of strategic minerals such as vanadium and titanium. Industry representatives sought technological hand-holding from CSIR laboratories for scaling these technologies, while the discussion also covered exploration possibilities for rare earths and other critical minerals in eastern India.
Dr. Jitendra Singh emphasised the need to leverage the capabilities being developed across CSIR institutions and other government scientific agencies.
The Minister also responded to industry inputs relating to space technology and specialised optical components. Dr. Jitendra Singh sought the relevant details and indicated that the space-related matter could be taken up with the Department of Space.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said that regulatory simplification had already been undertaken and invited further specific inputs from industry, which could be taken up for consideration.
Dr. Jitendra Singh suggested exploring a common R&D facility for the foundry sector, with the industry coming together to articulate its requirements and the government facilitating the platform.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said there was no restriction on industries coming together to create such a platform and urged steel-sector players to collaborate. “We are ready to provide the forum. You come, all of you from all the different steel industries, as representatives, come as a group and say, ‘Provide us a forum.’ We’ll provide,” he said.
Bengal Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals raised the possibility of reviving indigenous production of anti-snake venom, pointing out that eastern India has distinct snake species and therefore specific regional requirements.  Dr. Jitendra Singh advised the company to engage with the Health Ministry of W Bengal and stressed the importance of aligning any such effort with the scientific and public-health requirements.
A startup working in the venom and snakebite space subsequently presented technologies for identifying the species responsible for a snakebite and developing new antivenom solutions. Dr. Jitendra Singh welcomed the innovation but emphasised that such technologies would require proper scientific validation and clinical trials before wider adoption. He stressed that patient safety cannot be compromised and pointed the innovators towards the W Bengal Health Ministry for the necessary validation.
Throughout the interaction, Dr. Jitendra Singh repeatedly encouraged industry representatives to move from general discussions to specific, actionable requirements and assured that the government and scientific institutions would facilitate appropriate linkages. In his concluding remarks, he said, “You tell us what we can do for you or what we are not doing for you, or what we can do better for you,” underlining the government’s readiness to respond to clearly articulated industry needs.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also made it clear that such engagement should not remain restricted to formal events. “If there are further inputs, you are always free. Not that you have to wait for a formal occasion like this,” he said, inviting industry to continue engaging with the concerned institutions. The interaction at the 6th RISE Conclave thus reinforced a clear model for strengthening India’s technology ecosystem, industry as a partner from the beginning of R&D, scientific institutions as technology enablers, and government as a facilitator for taking promising technologies from the laboratory to the market and ultimately to wider societal application.

title: Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh Says RISE Conclave Puts Spotlight on India’s Tier-2 and Tier-3 Startup Powerhouse
subtitle:
RISE Conclave in Kolkata brings science, startups, industry and government together to accelerate lab-to-market journey of indigenous technologies

Four CSIR laboratories showcase capabilities across Minerals, Medicine, Materials and Machines; Startup Exhibition and S&T Pavilion provide platform for technology partnerships

Eight MoUs, four technology transfers, two product launches and one facility inauguration mark focus on translating research into tangible outcomes

67 experts across eight panels deliberate on healthcare, manufacturing, advanced materials, critical minerals, decarbonisation and science-driven startups
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 2:18PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, Minister of State for Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions, Department of Atomic Energy and Department of Space, Dr Jitendra Singh today called for taking India’s rapidly expanding startup ecosystem beyond metropolitan centres and creating stronger linkages between science, startups and industry to accelerate the journey of indigenous technologies from laboratories to the marketplace.
Addressing the inaugural session of the 6th RISE Conclave 2026 in Kolkata, Dr Jitendra Singh said there is a growing need to recognise the innovation potential of Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, noting that more than 50–60 per cent of India’s startups do not belong to metros. Young innovators from smaller cities are increasingly matching and, in several cases, excelling their counterparts in bigger cities, he said, making it important for scientific institutions and the innovation ecosystem to reach out to them rather than expecting them to travel to established technology hubs.
The Minister said the RISE Conclave provides precisely such a platform by bringing startups, industry representatives, potential mentors, researchers and government representatives under one roof. He said this convergence is essential for ensuring that scientific research is not confined to laboratories but moves towards entrepreneurship, technology transfer, commercialisation and wider societal application.
Dr Jitendra Singh said Kolkata’s selection as the venue for the RISE Conclave carries a special significance because of the city’s historic contribution to India’s scientific and academic journey. Recalling Bengal’s long tradition of scientific excellence and institution-building, he said Kolkata has produced and nurtured eminent personalities and institutions that have contributed significantly to India’s intellectual and scientific progress.
Referring to the legacy of Dr Bidhan Chandra Roy, Prof. U. N. Brahmachari, Sir C. V. Raman and Dr Syama Prasad Mukherjee, among others, Dr Jitendra Singh said the present generation has the responsibility to live up to this extraordinary legacy and help restore Kolkata’s position as a major centre of scientific and technological excellence. He said the city’s intellectual strength and academic aptitude provide a strong foundation for connecting its historic scientific heritage with frontier technologies and entrepreneurship.
Dr Jitendra Singh said the Government’s Whole-of-Government approach is increasingly translating into a Whole-of-Science approach, bringing different ministries, departments, research institutions, academia and industry together. He said the convergence of CSIR laboratories with institutions such as IIT Kharagpur, IISER Kolkata, NIT Durgapur and Atal Tinkering Labs, along with networks under the Department of Biotechnology, Department of Science and Technology, Department of Atomic Energy and Ministry of Earth Sciences, can create a strong knowledge corridor in eastern India.
The Minister said India has in recent years created new opportunities for private-sector participation in areas that were earlier largely closed to industry, including space, nuclear energy and biotechnology. The opening up of these sectors, he said, has created a new environment for startups and businesses to participate in national technology development.
Dr Jitendra Singh also referred to the Government’s decision to establish a ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund, as well as the role of the AnusandhanNational Research Foundation (ANRF), in encouraging high-risk, high-reward research and stronger partnerships among academia, startups and industry.
The Minister urged industry to come forward to adopt, support, finance and commercialise indigenous technologies emerging from Indian laboratories. He said scientific projects and startups cannot be sustained in isolation and require a mutually beneficial relationship with business and industry. For technologies to reach the market at scale, he added, industry must see clear commercial value and become an active partner in the innovation process.
Dr Jitendra Singh also stressed that the outcomes of RISE Conclave should become part of a larger and continuous innovation ecosystem, rather than remaining confined to a single event. He called for taking the knowledge, technologies and opportunities emerging from such platforms to wider sections of society through communication in languages and formats that people understand and access, enabling the learnings of one RISE edition to feed into the next.
The 6th RISE Conclave 2026, being held on September 6–7 at CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (CSIR-IICB), Salt Lake, Kolkata, is organised jointly by CSIR-CGCRI, CSIR-IICB, CSIR-CMERI and CSIR-IMMT under the theme “Driving Innovation & Entrepreneurship for Viksit Bharat 2047.” The conclave brings together startups, industry, academia, researchers, innovators, investors, incubators, MSMEs and policymakers to strengthen the interface between scientific research, entrepreneurship and industrial application.
The inaugural session was addressed by Dr N. Kalaiselvi, Director General, CSIR and Secretary, Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR). Dr SharadwatMukherjee, Minister-in-Charge, Department of Health and Family Welfare, Government of West Bengal, was the Guest of Honour. Prof. Vibha Tandon, Director, CSIR-IICB; Dr Ramanuj Narayan, Director, CSIR-IMMT; Prof. BikramjitBasu, Director, CSIR-CGCRI; Dr Naresh Chandra Murmu, Director, CSIR-CMERI; senior scientists, researchers, startup founders, industry representatives and other stakeholders were also present.
The Kolkata edition is the sixth edition of the RISE Conclave, following earlier editions in Mumbai, Lucknow, Hyderabad, Chennai and Bengaluru. Dr Jitendra Singh said taking the national RISE platform to different parts of the country is aimed at improving outreach and connecting scientific capabilities with innovators and entrepreneurs across regions.
At the centre of the conclave is the 4M framework: Minerals, Medicine, Materials and Machines, representing the complementary strengths of the four participating CSIR laboratories.
The participating CSIR laboratories also showcased indigenous technologies and products with potential for technology transfer, licensing, commercialisation and wider industrial application. The technologies span areas ranging from advanced materials, healthcare and machinery to sanitation, waste management and sustainable engineering solutions, demonstrating the potential of indigenous research to address both industrial and societal requirements.
The Startup Exhibition and S&T Pavilion provided a common platform for startups and entrepreneurs to showcase their technologies and products and engage with researchers, industry representatives, investors and dignitaries. The conclave brought together around 150 startups, with around 300 startup representatives and another 150 delegates from incubation and innovation centres forming part of the wider participation.
The technical programme comprises eight panel discussions involving 67 panelists, covering a wide range of issues including drug discovery and affordable healthcare; manufacturing technology, innovation and R&D for MSMEs; materials-led innovation; decarbonisation of steel and aluminium; critical minerals and new materials; science communication; opportunities for science-driven startups; and traditional wisdom and modern innovation.
A special lecture on “The Lab-to-Market Leap: Building Ventures from Breakthrough Research” further focuses on converting breakthrough research into ventures and market-oriented opportunities.
The conclave has also translated its focus on technology commercialisation into concrete outcomes, with eight Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) and four technology transfer initiatives forming a key part of the programme. The event also features the launch of two products and inauguration of one facility, along with the launch of the CGCRI’s new logo, compendium and Bootcamp.
An Industry Meet has brought senior industry representatives and other stakeholders together for interaction with scientists and dignitaries, with a focus on strengthening industry–research linkages and identifying opportunities for collaboration, technology adoption and commercialisation.
Dr Jitendra Singh said the scientific and technological strengths of eastern India, coupled with its strong academic and industrial base, can play a major role in India’s technology-led growth. He said startups can serve as key vehicles for technology transfer, while established industries in sectors such as steel, aluminium, mining, jute, IT and software can become important partners in taking indigenous technologies to scale.
He also called for greater use of artificial intelligence and digital technologies to add new capabilities to indigenous machines, optical networks and other technologies emerging from Indian laboratories, creating new opportunities for industry and startups.
The Minister said India’s recent progress across space, biotechnology, nuclear energy and digital economy, along with indigenous developments in areas such as vaccines, therapeutics and other advanced technologies, demonstrates the potential of a science ecosystem when government, academia and industry work together. He said the next phase of growth requires this integration to become deeper, wider and more sustained.
Dr Jitendra Singh said the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 requires India to combine its historic scientific legacy with indigenous technology, entrepreneurship, modern manufacturing and strong industry partnerships. He said the 6th RISE Conclave can serve as an important bridge between Bengal’s historic scientific spirit and the new energy of Indian entrepreneurship, helping the country to build, manufacture, heal and lead through indigenous innovation.
The conclave’s valedictory programme on September 7 includes an address by Dr Kalyan Chakraborti, Minister-in-Charge for Science and Technology and Biotechnology, Information Technology and Electronics, Food Processing Industries and Horticulture, Government of West Bengal.

title: Vibrant Villages Programme
subtitle: Strengthening India's Frontiers Through Inclusive Development
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                06 SEP 2026 11:00AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The
Vibrant Villages Programme (VVP
) has redefined the role of India's border villages. They are no longer remote outposts. They are now
strategic partners
in national security and development. The programme is implemented through
VVP-I
and
VVP-II
, with a combined outlay of
Rs
11,639 crore
. It is expanding road connectivity, electricity, telecommunications, healthcare, education and livelihood opportunities across villages along India's international land borders. VVP seeks to build vibrant, resilient and prosperous border communities. It improves quality of life and creates sustainable economic opportunities. In doing so, it strengthens India’s border security by sustaining thriving communities along its frontiers.
Why the Border Village Matters
India shares over
15,000 kilometres (km)
of international land border with seven neighbouring countries. The longest stretch runs
4,096.7 km
along the border with
Bangladesh
.
China
follows at
3,488 km
and
Pakistan
at
3,323 km
. Nepal, Myanmar, Bhutan and Afghanistan account for the remainder.
For decades, many border villages remained isolated by difficult terrain, weak connectivity, limited infrastructure and few livelihood opportunities. These challenges triggered out-migration, leaving several frontier areas sparsely populated. To address these longstanding issues, the
Vibrant Villages Programme (VVP)
was launched in
2023.
It seeks to accelerate the comprehensive development of selected villages along India's borders. Recognising border residents as the
eyes and ears
of the border guiding forces, it aims to build vibrant, secure and prosperous frontier communities.
The programme also marks a shift in perspective by treating these settlements
not as the nation's last villages, but as its first
.
Starting with northern border villages, the Government has expanded the programme across the entire land frontier in phases. Empowered border communities form the foundation of a
secure
and
strong Viksit Bharat@2047.
Did You Know?
The first warning of the 1999 Kargil intrusion did not come from a radar or a patrol. On 3 May 1999, local residents were the first to report suspicious movement in the Kargil sector. This underscores the importance of border communities as the first line of defence for the nation.
Two Phases, One Frontier Mission
The Government is implementing the Vibrant Villages Programme in two phases that together cover India's entire international land border.
VVP-I
covers villages along the northern border.
VVP-II
extends the same approach to the other international land borders. Together, the two phases aim to cover more than
2616 villages
with
a combined outlay of
Rs. 11,639 crore
.
The two phases differ in design but share a single purpose. VVP-I is a
Centrally Sponsored Scheme
implemented with the States, while VVP-II is a
Central Sector Scheme
funded fully by the Centre. Both phases of the initiative aim to improve
living conditions
,
generate local livelihoods
and
empower border communities
. They work to strengthen the nation's border security by developing "first villages" as vibrant centres of growth.
VVP-I:
Strengthening Northern Border Communities
The first phase of the
VVP
was announced in the Union Budget 2022-23 for villages along the northern border. It was launched at Kibithoo in Anjaw district of Arunachal Pradesh on 10 April 2023. The villages in 46 blocks abutting northern border in 4 States and 1 UT in
19 Districts
were identified out of which 662 strategic villages were taken on priority for comprehensive development covering a population of about 1.42 lakh.
These are
Arunachal Pradesh
,
Himachal Pradesh
,
Sikkim
,
Uttarakhand
and the Union Territory of
Ladakh
. The scheme was approved with an outlay of
Rs 4,800
crore. This covers the financial years
2022-23 to
2026-27
. Out
of this amount,
Rs 2,500
crore was earmarked for
road connectivity
. The programme aims to bridge the development gap in remote border villages. It strives to provide quality infrastructure and essential services to them comparable to those available elsewhere in the country.
Did You Know
?
Kibithoo
was chosen to launch the VVP due to its strategic location, history and development needs. Located in Arunachal Pradesh's Anjaw district, it is among India's easternmost inhabited villages. The area witnessed fierce fighting during the
1962 India–China War
. Remote terrain, sparse connectivity and out-migration have long constrained development. Launching the Programme from Kibithoo reflected the Government's vision of bringing development first to the nation's frontier.
Key interventions under VVP-I
The programme supports
all-weather roads, drinking water, reliable electricity, mobile and internet connectivity, and essential healthcare and education infrastructure
. It also promotes
tourism
facilities and multi-purpose
community centres
to improve livelihoods and the overall quality of life. Livelihood support is organised on a
hub-and-spoke model.
It encourages
social entrepreneurship, the empowerment of youth and women, the promotion of tourism and local culture, and one-
block-
one-product
enterprises. By creating convergence, VVP-I established the delivery model that the second phase now carries to the rest of the land border.
Did You Know?
India has been supporting border villages for nearly four decades. The
Border Area Development Programme (BADP)
was launched in
1986-87
along the western border. It was later expanded to cover villages within 10 km from the first habitation from international border. It covered 111 districts across 16 States and 2 Union Territories, and sanctioned over
39,000
development works since 2004-05. The programme is now in its sunset phase. Building on this foundation, VVP focuses on selected border villages. It ensures they receive every applicable government scheme, helping people stay in their villages and strengthen border security.
VVP-II: Extending the Model to All Land Borders
The Union Cabinet approved VVP-II on
2nd April, 2025. Unlike the first phase, VVP-II is funded entirely by the Centre and implemented by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). It was formally launched on
20th February, 2026 at Nathanpur village in Cachar district of Assam. The scheme carries an outlay of
Rs. 6,

Interventions under VVP-II
T

The scheme supports infrastructure, value chains through cooperatives and self-help groups (SHGs), SMART classrooms, tourism circuits and sustainable livelihoods. It also promotes road connectivity, healthcare, financial inclusion, skill development, and telecom connectivity.
The objective is to improve living conditions, generate livelihoods and encourage people to stay in border villages. It extends the Vibrant Villages Programme to India's entire land border under a unified development framework.

Delivering Development Through Scheme Convergence
The VVP implementation is guided by
Village Action Plans
. This is to be achieved through border-specific, State-specific and village-specific interventions based on local needs.
The programme follows
a convergence-based approach
, ensuring saturation of schemes under existing norms. All-weather roads are being developed under the
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY)-IV
of the Ministry of Rural Development.
Since the border villages face unique challenges, a High-Powered Committee chaired by the Cabinet Secretary may recommend relaxations in scheme guidelines to address them. The Ministry of Home Affairs is the nodal ministry. It works closely with State Governments, district administrations and border guarding forces for coordinated planning and implementation.

VVP: Impact Beyond Infrastructure
The impact of the Vibrant Villages Programme extends beyond infrastructure to strengthen security, livelihoods, governance and community resilience.
Security
:
A populated and confident border belt supports the work of the border-guarding forces. Both phases seek to create a strong frontier population acting as a strategic asset to the nation.
Demography & Reverse Migration:
Livelihood opportunities and improved connectivity give families reason to remain in the border villages. In Arunachal Pradesh, people of border villages of Kurung Kumey, Dibang Valley and Shi-Yomi districts are returning to their villages. This signifies the impact of the programme.
Economy:
Border tourism, cooperatives, SHGs and Farmer Producer Organisations are creating a local income base in areas where economic opportunity was previously limited. Local procurement by the border guarding forces adds an assured market within the village itself.
Governance:
The saturation approach brings every eligible household in these villages within the reach of existing Central and State schemes. Village Action Plans give the district administration a single instrument for sequencing that work across several departments.
Collectively, these four strands describe a single idea: that development and security are not competing claims on the frontier but reinforce one another.
Did You Know?
In Arunachal Pradesh, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) procures milk, vegetables, eggs and grains directly from vibrant villages. A border post thereby becomes a dependable customer for the farms beside it.
Towards a Connected and Self-Reliant Frontier
The Vibrant Villages Programme is a promise that India's frontier communities will share fully in the nation's progress. Better infrastructure, sustainable livelihoods and convergence of government schemes are creating opportunities closer to home. At the same time, border tourism and local enterprise are unlocking the region's potential. As these villages become more vibrant, prosperous and self-reliant, they will continue to strengthen India's borders and advance the vision of a secure, inclusive and
Viksit Bharat by 2047
.
